title: Why Intelligibility — Not Accent — Is the Goal
brief: Open by establishing that the aim of pronunciation teaching is communication, not the elimination of a learner's accent. Draw directly on the module's statement that pronunciation is valuable 'to the extent that it addresses learners' needs and does not impede the development of other skills or learning objectives,' and that a teacher 'can ignore the issue of pronunciation altogether if student pronunciation is not interfering with communication.' Use this to frame intelligibility as the practical, encouraging standard: if listeners understand the speaker, pronunciation is doing its job. Reassure trainee teachers that this framing reduces pressure on both teacher and student and keeps the focus on meaningful communication.

title: The Hidden Cost of Over-Correcting
brief: Explain why constant correction is counterproductive, drawing on the module's explicit warning that 'constantly interrupting students to correct minor pronunciation mistakes or patterns of errors may have the negative effect of undermining student's self-confidence or preventing the development of oral fluency.' Connect this to the broader principle that oral fluency needs space to develop. Encourage trainee teachers to distinguish between errors that genuinely block communication and minor deviations that do not, and to reserve correction for the former. Keep the tone practical and reassuring rather than prescriptive.

title: Listening First: Identifying What Actually Needs Work
brief: Describe how a teacher can use careful, attentive listening during group work and other activities to spot genuine pronunciation problems before deciding whether to act. Base this on the module's guidance that 'through careful listening, a teacher can identify problematic pronunciation patterns' and that a teacher 'can predict the kinds of sounds, words, and intonation that may be problematic' for particular learners. Explain that this diagnostic listening step — done while circulating among groups — allows the teacher to make informed, targeted decisions rather than reacting to every error in the moment. Emphasise that prediction (anticipating likely problem areas before a lesson) is also a useful planning tool.

title: Core Techniques: Modelling, Drilling, and Minimal Pairs
brief: Introduce the main classroom techniques for pronunciation work. Draw on the module's reference to the 'repeat after me' activity as a way to 'model and practice pronunciation,' and to students practicing dialogues and listening to recordings while completing tasks. Use these as the basis for explaining modeling and drilling. Introduce minimal pairs and listen-and-discriminate activities as ways to sharpen learners' ability to hear and produce distinctions that matter for intelligibility. Keep descriptions concrete and classroom-ready, with brief illustrative examples of how each technique works in practice.

title: Integrating Pronunciation into Normal Lessons
brief: Show trainee teachers how pronunciation work fits naturally inside regular lessons rather than requiring separate, dedicated time. Draw on the module's recommendation that a teacher 'can take a short amount of time to practice correct pronunciation with students at periodic intervals without interrupting the students' group work.' Connect this to the module's broader point that skills are 'reinforced through meaningful repetition' when embedded in a coherent lesson context. Offer practical suggestions for weaving brief pronunciation moments into activities already planned — vocabulary introduction, role-plays, and discussion tasks — so that pronunciation never feels like an interruption or an add-on.

title: Building Confidence: A Practical Mindset for Teachers
brief: Close the unit by addressing the trainee teacher's own confidence in handling pronunciation. Revisit the module's point that pronunciation teaching should not 'impede the development of other skills or learning objectives,' reinforcing that a light, strategic touch is both acceptable and effective. Draw on the module's framing of teacher development as a cycle of observing, evaluating, adapting, and acting to encourage teachers to experiment with pronunciation techniques, reflect on what works, and refine their approach over time. End with an encouraging reminder that the goal is always communication: when students are understood, the teaching is working.
